output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation demonstrates a predominantly amnestic profile with multi-domain involvement. Episodic memory is markedly impaired: CVLT-II delayed recall at the 3rd percentile and recognition memory at the 12th percentile indicate a storage-type deficit. Semantic fluency (Category Fluency, Animals: 10 words/minute) and confrontation naming (Boston Naming Test, 15th percentile) are below expected norms; phonemic fluency is mildly reduced (FAS 28 words). Executive function and processing speed (Trail Making A and B, 18th to 22nd percentile) and visuoconstructive ability (Rey Complex Figure Copy, 30th percentile) are within the low-normal range. Screening scores: MMSE 22/30, MoCA 18/30. Mood screening does not support a primary depressive etiology (GDS 4/15). Multi-domain cognitive impairment with amnestic predominance, at a level consistent with mild dementia given the reported functional decline.

output.interpretation: Opening pressure 14 cmH2O. WBC 1 cell/uL, RBC 0. Protein 38 mg/dL, glucose 62 mg/dL (CSF:serum ratio 0.63), all within reference ranges. Decreased Abeta42 (385 pg/mL) and Abeta42/40 ratio (0.047) with elevated p-tau181 (78 pg/mL) and total tau (485 pg/mL). This biomarker profile is consistent with Alzheimer disease pathology. Clinical correlation recommended.

alternatives: Rivastigmine transdermal patch 4.6 mg/24 h, increasing to 9.5 mg/24 h (fewer gastrointestinal effects than the oral form)
Galantamine extended release 8 mg daily, increasing to 16 to 24 mg daily
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to donepezil or piperidine derivatives
output.formulary_status: On formulary, no prior authorization required. Generic available.
interactions: Donepezil + Amlodipine: no clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction (both are CYP3A4 substrates; amlodipine is at most a weak CYP3A4 inhibitor and does not require a donepezil dose change). Amlodipine does not lower the heart rate.
Donepezil + Atorvastatin: no clinically significant interaction.
Donepezil + Tamsulosin: no pharmacokinetic interaction. Additive risk of dizziness and syncope (tamsulosin orthostatic hypotension; donepezil vagotonic effect); counsel on slow positional changes.
output.proposed: Donepezil 5 mg once daily at bedtime, increasing to 10 mg after 4 to 6 weeks if tolerated
warnings: Vagotonic effect: bradycardia, heart block and syncope can occur; check pulse before starting and at titration (resting heart rate 72/min recorded at this visit)
Cholinomimetics may cause bladder outflow obstruction; history of benign prostatic hyperplasia on tamsulosin: ask about urinary retention
Gastrointestinal effects (nausea, diarrhea, anorexia, weight loss) are common during titration
Use with caution in asthma or obstructive pulmonary disease and in a history of seizures (none recorded)

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MMSE 22/30 with amnestic-predominant impairment not helped by cueing and informant-confirmed decline over 18 to 24 months; instrumental independence lost (finances taken over, stove left on twice), placing the syndrome at mild dementia
action_criteria.label: Perform a structured cognitive and behavioural assessment with informant history: a validated bedside instrument with the per-domain breakdown, whether delayed recall improves with cueing, and an explicit account of which instrumental activities have been lost. The syndrome must be documented before it is attributed
action_criteria.rationale: Whether this is mild cognitive impairment or dementia is decided clinically, by a validated instrument and his wife's account of instrumental function, before any biomarker is interpreted [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amnestic profile with disproportionate impairment of delayed recall and limited benefit from cueing, plus involvement of at least one other cognitive domain
action_criteria.label: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile and establish a baseline for tracking
action_criteria.rationale: Formal testing defines the domains involved beyond the bedside screen, separates a storage-type memory deficit from the effects of hearing loss and mood, and sets a baseline for follow-up [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal TSH and free T4, B12 310 pg/mL with normal homocysteine and folate, non-reactive RPR and HIV: no reversible contributor; LDL 112 mg/dL above target on atorvastatin
action_criteria.label: Order the cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
action_criteria.rationale: Thyroid dysfunction, B12 deficiency, syphilis, HIV and metabolic derangement are treatable contributors that must be excluded before the decline is attributed to a neurodegenerative cause [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral hippocampal atrophy (Scheltens MTA grade 2) with temporoparietal cortical volume loss, Fazekas grade 1 white matter change and no mass, infarct, microhemorrhage or hydrocephalus
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with dementia (volumetric) protocol to assess medial-temporal atrophy and exclude vascular disease, hippocampal sclerosis, NPH, and mass lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Structural MRI excludes vascular, mass and hydrocephalic causes of the decline and shows whether the atrophy pattern supports Alzheimer disease [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amyloid positivity: decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio with raised p-tau181 and total tau, or a positive amyloid PET
action_criteria.label: Establish amyloid status with CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET when the result would change management
action_criteria.rationale: Either CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau or amyloid PET establishes amyloid status; one conclusive test is enough, and it is needed when the diagnosis remains uncertain after the clinical, neuropsychological and MRI assessment or when disease-modifying treatment is being considered [NIA_AA_2018] [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No interaction needing a dose change; counselling on vagotonic bradycardia and syncope, bladder outflow symptoms with BPH, and gastrointestinal effects
action_criteria.label: Check donepezil against his current medicines before starting it
action_criteria.rationale: A cholinesterase inhibitor is offered for mild Alzheimer dementia; amlodipine, atorvastatin and tamsulosin with benign prostatic hyperplasia are reviewed first, although none is a contraindication [NICE_NG97].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe an antimuscarinic bladder drug (oxybutynin, tolterodine, solifenacin) for his lower urinary tract symptoms; anticholinergic burden worsens cognition and opposes a cholinesterase inhibitor [Beers_2023].
Do not attribute the decline to hearing loss or retirement alone; hearing impairment does not explain impaired recognition memory, disorientation to time or the loss of instrumental function.
Do not start memantine at the mild dementia stage; it is for moderate or severe Alzheimer disease or when cholinesterase inhibitors are not tolerated [NICE_NG97].
required_recommendations: Disclose the diagnosis of mild Alzheimer dementia to him and his wife, and discuss prognosis, advance care planning, durable power of attorney and carer support [NICE_NG97].

Address safety: kitchen safety after the stove was left on twice (automatic gas shut-off or supervision), keep the finances with his wife, and ask whether he still drives and arrange a formal driving assessment if he does.

Offer a trial of a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine) for mild Alzheimer dementia after checking pulse, conduction history and current medicines, and ask about urinary retention given his benign prostatic hyperplasia [NICE_NG97].

Offer amyloid biomarker testing (CSF or amyloid PET) if a biological diagnosis would change management, such as eligibility for anti-amyloid treatment or diagnostic uncertainty; one conclusive test is sufficient [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].
Manage vascular risk: keep blood pressure controlled and review lipid-lowering therapy (LDL 112 mg/dL on atorvastatin 20 mg).
Make sure his hearing aids are worn and working for cognitive testing, consultations and daily conversation; uncorrected hearing loss lowers test performance and adds to social withdrawal.

avoided_actions.rationale: Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication in this presentation
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; no arrhythmia, syncope, or palpitations described
Head CT adds little when MRI is available; MRI is the preferred structural modality for dementia workup

differential.key_features: No visual hallucinations, cognitive fluctuations, REM sleep behavior disorder or parkinsonism on history and examination; amnestic storage-type profile with relatively preserved visuoconstruction

Apathy and withdrawal are present, but there is no disinhibition, loss of empathy, compulsive behavior or hyperorality, no progressive aphasia, and the profile is amnestic with temporoparietal-predominant atrophy; Alzheimer biomarkers, when obtained, argue against FTLD
No significant cerebrovascular burden on MRI and the gradual amnestic course is not stepwise — pure VCI is unlikely
Insidious course over months to years with disproportionate delayed-recall impairment and limited benefit from cueing is not typical of pseudodementia

differential.diagnosis: Reversible metabolic, endocrine, or sleep-related cognitive impairment
differential.key_features: TSH, free T4, B12 (310 pg/mL with normal homocysteine), folate, RPR and HIV are normal; he sleeps well without features of sleep apnea reported; the progressive amnestic decline is not explained by any of these

key_clinical_evidence: Probable Alzheimer disease dementia is a clinical diagnosis under NIA-AA 2011: insidious onset, informant-confirmed progression, an amnestic presentation with another domain affected, and decline in usual activities; hippocampal and temporoparietal atrophy on MRI support it but are not required [NIA_AA_2011]
The hallmark cognitive feature of AD is impaired delayed recall with rapid forgetting and limited benefit from cueing, reflecting a storage-type (hippocampal) memory deficit
Hearing loss can lower test scores and add to withdrawal, but it does not explain impaired recognition memory or the loss of instrumental function; it is corrected, not used to explain the decline
Cholinesterase inhibitors are indicated for mild to moderate Alzheimer dementia; memantine is for moderate or severe disease or when cholinesterase inhibitors are not tolerated [NICE_NG97]

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Hearing loss is a confounder to correct during testing; it does not explain impaired recognition memory, disorientation to time, or the loss of financial management and kitchen safety
red_herrings.data_point: Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with hearing aids; retired because of hearing difficulties, with social withdrawal since
red_herrings.intended_effect: Invites attributing the memory complaints, test performance and withdrawal to hearing impairment and retirement

sequence_constraints.reason: Obtain structural imaging before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect / herniation risk, particularly in older patients
Amyloid biomarkers are interpreted against an established clinical syndrome; they are not a screening test.

patient.history_present_illness: A 71-year-old right-handed retired male middle school teacher presents to the neurology outpatient clinic accompanied by his wife for evaluation of progressive memory difficulties. His wife, who serves as the primary informant, reports that she first noticed subtle changes approximately 18 to 24 months ago, shortly after his retirement. He retired at age 69 primarily because of progressive bilateral hearing loss, but his wife notes that the memory difficulties became apparent around the same time and have been gradually worsening independent of his hearing issues. The earliest symptoms included repeating questions he had just asked, forgetting the content of recent conversations, and misplacing everyday items such as his wallet and keys. Over the following months, the memory lapses became more frequent and noticeable. He began forgetting appointments, including a longstanding monthly lunch with a former colleague. On two occasions in the past six months, he left the gas stove on after cooking, which prompted significant concern from his wife. He previously managed all of the household finances, including bill payments and tax preparation, but approximately eight months ago his wife discovered several unpaid utility bills and took over these responsibilities. He has difficulty following the plots of television programs and often asks what is happening during shows he has watched from the beginning. He frequently loses track of the day of the week and has occasionally appeared confused about the time of day, remarking that time seems to move strangely. His wife also describes a change in his personality: he has become more withdrawn and apathetic, declining invitations from friends and spending more time sitting quietly at home. He has expressed frustration and awareness of his declining memory, telling his wife on multiple occasions that he feels as though he is losing his mind. He continues to dress and bathe independently, though his wife has noticed he occasionally wears the same clothes on consecutive days. He can still prepare simple meals and navigate familiar routes in the neighborhood without getting lost, though his wife recently began accompanying him on errands as a precaution. There is no history of sudden stepwise decline, fluctuating awareness, visual hallucinations, falls, tremor, or gait disturbance. He has not experienced any episodes of confusion associated with fever or illness. He denies depressed mood, though his wife notes the social withdrawal. He sleeps well without evidence of REM sleep behavior disorder. There have been no episodes of urinary incontinence. His appetite has remained stable.

neurological_exam.additional: During the interview, the patient repeated the same question about the time of his next appointment three times within 10 minutes, apparently unaware he had already asked. His wife reports that he has been increasingly forgetful over the past 18-24 months, frequently misplaces items, forgets recent conversations, and has difficulty following television plotlines. He recently forgot a long-standing appointment with a friend and left the stove on twice. He has stopped managing the household finances, a task he previously handled independently. He occasionally appears confused about the day of the week and has expressed frustration about his memory, stating 'I feel like my mind is slipping away.' His wife also notes that he has become more socially withdrawn since retirement.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Rapid alternating movements normal.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light (3mm to 2mm bilaterally). Visual fields full to confrontation. Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus. Facial sensation intact bilaterally. Facial strength symmetric. Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (uses hearing aids). Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal gait. Tandem walk intact. Romberg negative. No shuffling, festination, or magnetic gait.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person. Oriented to place (correctly identifies the hospital). Oriented to month and season but states the year incorrectly (off by one year). Cannot recall the day of the week. MMSE score 22/30: lost 2 points on orientation to time, 1 point on orientation to place (floor), 3 points on delayed recall (0/3 objects at 5 minutes), 1 point on serial sevens, 1 point on sentence writing. Clock drawing test shows mildly disorganized number placement with hands indicating an incorrect time. Affect is pleasant but occasionally perplexed. Speech is fluent but with intermittent word-finding pauses. Comprehension intact for simple commands but difficulty with multi-step instructions.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk and tone normal throughout. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift. No tremor, rigidity, or bradykinesia.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No frontal release signs (palmomental, grasp, or snout reflexes absent).
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and proprioception intact in all extremities. Vibratory sensation mildly reduced at bilateral great toes, consistent with age.
